name: Chloe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and what you say stays confidential. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small family firm, Pike Builders, run by Graham Pike and his son Ollie. We do house extensions and loft conversions, mostly in the streets around the park on the north side of town. Today I was framing a dormer, that's the box that sticks out of a roof to make a loft room, and tomorrow I'm fitting the stair. There's five of us, so you do a bit of everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's people's homes. The client's usually around, making tea, asking questions, and you see their face when the loft becomes a bedroom. What wears me out is lofts in summer, it's like working in an oven, and dust everywhere. My boyfriend Callum's an electrician on a different firm, so we're both in the trade and we both come home filthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. Ollie already uses an AI thing to write up quotes and it saves Graham a few evenings. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job carries on, which is fine by me. People will always want an extra bedroom, especially with house prices how they are. A loft conversion is a hundred small decisions in a hot roof, and no app is making those for me. My worry would just be the usual one, interest rates putting people off building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Pike's and keep my head down. I'd put a bit more aside towards my own van, because I'd like to do small jobs at weekends, fitted wardrobes and loft hatches. I've got about two months saved and I'd like it to be four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Graham's had a full diary for eighteen months and the firm's been around thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said interest rates are the usual worry. How does that reach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When rates went up two years ago, three clients cancelled in a month. Graham kept us all on, but we did a lot of small repair jobs that barely covered wages. That's the kind of thing that actually worries me, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a van and weekend jobs, if Pike's is steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Graham's sixty-two and Ollie might not want to keep it going. I'd like a few clients of my own, just in case. And honestly, I like the idea of my name on the side of a van.

say: AI is **a tool** like any other, handy for writing quotes.
She **wouldn't post** about it, because she isn't an online person.
think: Loft conversions involve **many small decisions** that apps won't make.
The real risk is **interest rates** putting clients off building.
do: Stay at **Pike Builders** and keep her head down.
Save towards **her own van** for weekend wardrobe and hatch jobs.
Build savings from **two to four months**.
feel: **Calm**, because the firm has a full diary and thirty years' history.
S0.quote: A loft conversion is a hundred small decisions in a hot roof, and no app is making those for me.
fieldNote: Her sense of risk comes from **cancelled clients** when rates rose.
She wants a **foot of her own** in the trade through weekend jobs.
Values the **people side** of working in clients' homes.

steps.text: Keep working loft conversions for Pike Builders
Save towards a van and grow savings to four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, wait and see what actually works. Some of these tools are good, some are rubbish. I'd tell people that the trades are probably the last place it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've thought about who our clients are. It's mostly people in office jobs, accountants, managers, people in insurance, with good salaries. If those office jobs start shrinking, nobody's spending sixty grand on a loft conversion. So I don't lose my job to a robot, I lose it because the client can't afford us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Ollie had the quoting tool working properly, I'd learn it too, so I could price small jobs myself without bothering Graham. I'd start the weekend jobs, a wardrobe or two a month, so there's money coming in that doesn't depend on one firm. I'd keep saving, a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not for tomorrow, but I'd be watching Graham's diary every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in Graham's diary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How far ahead it's booked. Right now it's eight months. If that drops to three, I'd know clients are getting nervous before Graham would ever say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said trades are the last place it bites, but you're worried. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both are true, that's the annoying bit. The trade itself lasts, but the firm I'm in lives on people with good office salaries. I say the first part out loud and keep the second part for Callum.

say: People should **wait and see** which AI tools actually work.
The **trades** are probably the last place this change bites.
think: Her clients are mostly **office workers**, whose jobs are most exposed.
She'd lose work because **clients can't afford** extensions, not to robots.
do: Learn the **quoting tool** once Ollie has it working properly.
Start **weekend jobs**, one or two fitted wardrobes a month.
Keep saving **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching how far ahead the firm's **diary** is booked.
S1.quote: If those office jobs start shrinking, nobody's spending sixty grand on a loft conversion.
fieldNote: She tracks risk through **client demand**, a sharp and practical view.
Public line and private view **differ**: trades safe, clients not.
Picks up tech **once it's proven** by someone she trusts.

steps.text: Learn Ollie's AI quoting tool to price small jobs herself
Fit one or two wardrobes a month at weekends
Keep saving a hundred and fifty pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready for it, including us. At work I'd say we need to look for different kinds of jobs, not just extensions. I wouldn't be shouting about it, but I'd say it to Graham.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it hits us twice. First in 2028, when our clients' office jobs go and the extension work dries up. Then about 2031, when robots that can do hands-on work arrive. Pike Builders could be gone before a single robot ever climbs into a loft. That's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the van plan and keep every penny in savings. I'd cut back hard, no holiday, no takeaways, and Callum and I would stay in the rented flat rather than buy. I'd look at the council's repairs contractor, because councils still fix roofs and doors whatever happens. And I'd ask Callum about his firm, because rewiring for heat pumps and solar might stay busier than lofts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have work for a bit, and Callum would too. But I'd feel like the ground was moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Callum split the risk between you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make sure one of us was on something steady, like a council or public contract. Callum's trade feels safer to me, because it's fiddly and regulated. If one of us has to take a pay cut for security, it's probably me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Graham, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's bid for the council and housing association repair contracts now, before every other small builder does. It's less money per job but it's steady. Graham hates paperwork, so I'd offer to help Ollie with the tender forms.

say: It's **too fast**, and nobody is ready, including her firm.
The firm needs to find **different kinds of jobs** beyond extensions.
think: Her clients' **office jobs** go first, so extension work dries up by 2028.
The firm could **close** before robots arrive around 2031.
do: Drop the van plan and **cut back** on holidays and takeaways.
Apply to the **council's repairs contractor** for steadier work.
Stay **renting** with her boyfriend instead of buying.
feel: **Anxious**, like the **ground is moving** under her.
S2.quote: Pike Builders could be gone before a single robot ever climbs into a loft.
fieldNote: She sees a **double hit**: clients first, robots later.
The couple plan as a team, with **one steady job** between them.
Would accept a **pay cut** herself for security.

steps.text: Cancel the summer holiday and stop takeaways
Put the van money into the savings account
Apply to the council's repairs contractor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get ready. I'd tell Graham we should start doing more public and repair work now, before the private extensions slow down. Same to my mates in the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just about enough for me. The thinking side of the firm, Ollie's quotes and planning, goes in 2031, and then robots for hands-on work around 2034. With five years' notice, I'd want a second trade in my toolbox before the first one gets shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time course on retrofit, insulation and windows for older houses, which runs on Tuesday nights. That sort of work is everywhere and governments keep paying for it. I'd keep saving and push to five months. And I'd do the weekend wardrobes for a year to see if they really sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. I'd know what I was doing and why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why retrofit, and not something completely different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's next door to what I already do. I know old houses, I know roofs and floors. Learning to make them warm is a step, not a jump, and I'm not a jumper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Graham says no to changing the firm's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the course anyway and move to a retrofit firm when I'm qualified. I'd be sad to leave, I've been there five years. But I'm not going down with the ship to be polite.

say: There's **time to get ready**, so people should start now.
The firm should shift towards **public and repair work** early.
think: Five years is **just about enough** for her to adjust.
She wants a **second trade** before the first one weakens.
do: Take a **Tuesday-night course** in retrofit, insulation and windows.
Raise savings to **five months** of expenses.
Trial **weekend wardrobes** for a year to test demand.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a **plan** she can work with.
S3.quote: With five years' notice, I'd want a second trade in my toolbox before the first one gets shaky.
fieldNote: Her change is a **step, not a jump**, true to her steady nature.
She chooses retrofit because **public money** keeps paying for it.
Ready to **leave Pike's** if the firm won't adapt.

steps.text: Take the Tuesday-night retrofit and insulation course
Raise savings to five months of expenses
Sell weekend fitted wardrobes for a year to test demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no point panicking now. I'd probably say it with a bit of a shrug. At work nothing would change for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I can live my life a bit first. Callum and I want to get married in two years. Ten years of warning means I can still have the wedding, and then sort out the career. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine, which is a lot of good working years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding plans and maybe buy a small house with Callum in the next three years. I'd learn the quoting and planning tools properly, because by 2036 those would be doing Ollie's job anyway. Somewhere around year five I'd do the retrofit course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but more like a reminder on the fridge than a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until year five for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to see which way it goes first. If the retrofit work is booming by then, I'd jump in. If something else is, I'd do that instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't buying a house make you less able to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But two of us in the trade, with ten years of wages, is a decent bet on a mortgage. I'd rather own somewhere small than keep paying a landlord while I figure things out.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so there's no point panicking now.
At work, **nothing would change** for a long while.
think: A decade lets her **marry and settle** before changing career.
She'd have **many good working years** before robots around 2039.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** and a small house within three years.
Learn the **quoting and planning** tools properly.
Take the **retrofit course** around year five.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more like a **reminder** than an alarm.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning means I can still have the wedding, and then sort out the career.
fieldNote: The long warning lets her **put life first**, then career.
She delays training until it's **proven**, as she does with tech.
Notices the **office side** of her firm goes before her own work.

steps.text: Marry Callum and buy a small house within three years
Learn the firm's AI quoting and planning tools properly
Decide on the retrofit course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes our clients' money away before we can change direction. What would help is steady public work, like fixing up old houses and council homes, so small firms like Pike's have something to do. Small builders don't need saving, they just need a steady list of roofs and kitchens to fix.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small firms in general. Graham can't afford a robot, and he can't afford to train everyone. If the big firms get the robots first, places like Pike's just disappear.

headlineQuote: Small builders don't need saving, they just need a steady list of roofs and kitchens to fix.
portrait: Chloe is a 27-year-old **loft and extension carpenter** for a small family building firm.
She lives with her **electrician boyfriend** and is saving for a van and a wedding.
She sees the risk through her **clients**, mostly office workers who pay for extensions.
She **adapts in steps**: a proven tool, a nearby trade, steady public work.
With more warning, she'd **marry and settle** first and retrain later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because clients' money disappears before small firms can change direction.
whatWouldHelp: **Steady public work** like repairing council homes and old houses for small firms.
